name: THE MO, LARRY, AND CURRY BURGER

recipe.history:
Yellow curry — and more specifically the blend of spices that creates its signature warm, golden character — is one of the most complex culinary inheritances in human history, with roots that extend back thousands of years across the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. The word 'curry' itself is a British colonial simplification of the Tamil word kari, used to describe a spiced sauce or relish served with rice, and the British East India Company systematically reduced an enormously diverse and regionally specific tradition of spiced cooking into a single exported concept that bore little resemblance to the subcontinental reality. Turmeric — the rhizome that gives yellow curry its vivid golden color — has been cultivated in India for at least four thousand years, revered as much for its medicinal and ritual properties as for its flavor. Cumin, coriander, fenugreek, mustard seed, and turmeric form the backbone of most yellow curry preparations, whether in the drier masala powders of northern India, the coconut-milk-enriched curries of Sri Lanka and South India, or the lemongrass-forward yellow curries of Thailand, where the spice blend was adapted through centuries of trade and cultural exchange along the maritime Silk Road.

Yellow curry made its entry into American cuisine through several distinct channels: the post-World War II immigration of South and Southeast Asian communities to major American cities, the influence of British curry culture on American food through the mid-twentieth century, and the explosion of pan-Asian restaurant culture in the 1980s and 1990s. Thai yellow curry in particular found enormous popular success in the United States because its coconut milk base softened the heat and introduced a sweetness that American palates found immediately accessible. The leap from curry as a restaurant dish to curry as a condiment and burger flavoring is a story of the American cook's instinct to use what is delicious in one context to transform another — yellow curry aioli began appearing on gourmet burger menus in the early 2010s as chefs recognized that the spice blend's warmth, depth, and fat-compatibility made it one of the best possible sauces for beef.

I have a specific memory attached to yellow curry and it lives in a small Thai restaurant in a strip mall that I drove forty minutes out of my way to visit at least twice a month for years. The yellow curry there came in a clay pot with one large potato and three pieces of chicken, and it was the color of a ripe mango and smelled like cardamom and coconut and something toasted and ancient. I started adding curry powder to mayonnaise at home immediately after the first time I ate there, working backward from the flavor I wanted to recreate — which I never did, because the original was beyond recreating, but the aioli I built in the attempt turned out to be its own extraordinary thing. That aioli is the core of this burger, and every time I make it I am in that clay pot in that strip mall, which is not the worst place to be.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is both a technical and philosophical commitment, and nowhere is that commitment more important than in a burger where a spiced, aromatic sauce is the star. The curry aioli and the curry-spiced caramelized onions are bold, complex, warm flavors, and they require a patty with enough moisture and structural integrity to stand up to them and participate in the conversation. A medium-rare patty accomplishes this: its pink interior has retained the gelatin and fat that keep it loose and juicy, and its deep brown exterior crust provides the Maillard-reaction depth of flavor that balances the sweetness of the curry and the onions. Overcook the patty and what you have is a flavor delivery vessel that has been stripped of its own identity — and a great burger is not a vehicle for sauce, it is a conversation between the beef and everything surrounding it. Medium rare keeps the beef in the conversation.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cubed
2 tablespoons black and white sesame seeds for topping
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
1/4 cup coconut oil, melted and cooled
3 large yellow onions, halved and thinly sliced
6 slices aged yellow cheddar (about 1 oz each)
1/2 English cucumber, sliced paper-thin on a mandoline
instructions: 1. MAKE THE SESAME BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, warm water, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.

2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes. Increase to medium and mix 6 minutes. Add softened butter one cube at a time on medium speed, incorporating fully, about 8 to 10 minutes. Increase to medium-high and mix 6 to 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover tightly, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 12 hours).
4. Next day, divide dough into 6 equal portions. Shape into tight round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 2 to 3 hours at room temperature.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat remaining egg with 1 tablespoon water. Brush buns with egg wash. Sprinkle generously with sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.
6. MAKE THE YELLOW CURRY AIOLI: Toast curry powder, turmeric, cumin, ground ginger, and cayenne in a dry skillet over medium-low heat for 60 to 90 seconds until fragrant. Cool completely.

7. Whisk egg yolks and mustard in a medium bowl. Whisk in garlic paste. Stream in neutral oil very slowly, whisking constantly, until the emulsion forms and thickens. Stream in melted cooled coconut oil. Whisk in lime juice and honey. Whisk in the toasted spice blend. Season with kosher salt. Taste and adjust lime and spice. Refrigerate until needed.

8. MAKE THE CURRY-SPICED CARAMELIZED ONIONS: Melt butter with oil in a wide heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Add onions and salt. Cook, stirring every 5 to 8 minutes, for 40 to 45 minutes until golden and soft. Add curry powder, cumin, coriander, turmeric, and brown sugar. Stir to coat the onions. Add water or broth and stir to incorporate. Cook 5 to 8 more minutes until deeply fragrant and jammy. Set aside.

9. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground lamb. Season with salt, pepper, cumin, and coriander. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
10. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes first side for a deep brown crust.

11. Flip once. Lay a slice of aged cheddar on each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
12. TOAST THE BUNS: Split buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds until golden.
13. DRESS THE GREENS: Toss baby spinach, cucumber, cilantro, and mint with lime juice and olive oil. Season with a pinch of salt just before assembly.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread curry aioli generously on both cut sides of each bun. Place dressed greens on the bottom bun. Add the rested, cheese-topped patty.
15. Spoon a generous mound of curry-spiced caramelized onions over the patty. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
